newsitem.title: UK: Sterling vaults to six-year highs against mark.
newsitem.headline: Sterling vaults to six-year highs against mark.

text.p: Sterling vaulted over 2.98 marks for the first time in six years on Friday as traders proved unable to resist the lure of higher UK interest rates.
Initial disappointment that UK rates rose by only a quarter-percentage point yesterday proved short-lived given expectations that more increases are on the way.

This made psychological targets such as three marks to the pound irresistible magnets for short-term traders. Longer-term investors are, however, wary of piling in after a year-long rally which has boosted sterling 30 percent against the mark.

"Trader are going for big levels like three against the mark and 1.70 against the dollar because the Bank of England has no choice but to raise rates," said Ian Winship, a fund manager at Scottish Amicable Investment Managers in Glasgow. "But I'd rather not buy gilts or sterling for my overseas accounts right now as I'm too nervous about it swinging around."

The pound rose as high as 2.9870 marks, the strongest it has been since April 1991. It was at 2.9848/58 at 1030 GMT from 2.9566/76 late Thursday in Europe. Cable also surged, climbing to $1.6980, its best showing since January 10. It was last at $1.6967/78 from $1.6882/92 Thursday.

A potent cocktail of strong consumption data, a budget which was viewed as being too soft on the British consumer, and an increase in the government's preferred measure of inflation have fuelled the latest leg of sterling's rally.

"The budget made it difficult to assess how high rates will have to go to contain the consumer mini-boom," said Steve Hannah, the director of economic research at IBJ International. "Given the issue of higher UK rates has not gone away, there is more sterling strength to come."
At 6.75 percent, UK base rates are already the highest of any major industrial nation and above most European Union rates.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer indicated Thursday that policy makers outside the UK view sterling's rise as justified. He said the pound's strength reflected economic fundamentals and interest rate expectations. Traders agree.

"Sterling is a buy on any kind of retracement and three marks looks pretty close now," said a currency trader in London. "Investors may be long but there are not too many interbank people who are too long given the way the market has been trading."
Also, the premium UK gilts offer over their EU counterparts is also beginning to look attractive.
UK bonds have failed to keep pace with gains Italian and Spanish bonds have racked up amid expectations a broad group of countries will launch European economic and monetary union.

Expectations Britain will not join EMU from the outset may have handicapped the UK bond market, but they have benefited sterling. Concern that the planned European single currency will not be as strong as the mark and the fact that the pound is not tied to the mark in the European exchange-rate mechanism has helped the pound climb against a broad range of currencies.
Sterling's trade-weighted index has surged 24 percent since August and is now at its highest since October 1990.

This strength may eventually prove to be sterling's undoing, though, some analysts warned. The damage that sterling's rally is inflicting on UK exporters will eventually boost Britain's trade deficit and could force the Bank of England to intervene in the open market to curb its strength, they said.
Traders are not yet concerned, though.

"The Bank has to do something to stop sterling's rise, but it probably does not want to show its hand at the moment," the London-based trader said. "Also, they will have learnt their lesson from years past and will not want to take the market on aggressively."
A bigger risk for sterling could be concern that German officials are beginning to voice about the mark's slump against the dollar.

A reversal in the dollar's surge to 41-month highs against the mark will make it easier for cable to hit the highs traders are targeting, but it will keep the magic three-marks-per-pound rate out of the grasp of sterling bulls.
